L01.why: Active 'has preserved' needs a singular agent and an object; passive or plural forms seem likelier for a preserved-thing subject, but any could fit some sentence.

L02.why: 'did' as an auxiliary is the least common fit, but every auxiliary here is grammatical in some sentence.

L03.why: Bare plural active 'repeatedly seal' needs a plural agent subject; each option fits some subject, so nothing is ruled out.

L04.why: Two colons framing an appositive and then a colon directly before 'and' is never standard punctuation.

L05.why: Future perfect 'will have been dismissed' is the rarest fit, but a future-reference sentence could need it.

L06.why: Tense and number depend entirely on the hidden subject and time frame; none can be excluded.

L07.why: No punctuation between 'oxygen' and 'any' usually fuses clauses, though 'oxygen any longer' shows it can be correct.

L08.why: Past perfect 'had kept out' needs an earlier-past frame; every tense here fits some sentence.

L09.why: Past perfect passive is the least likely, but voice and tense depend on the withheld subject.

L10.why: A semicolon before a quoted title only works inside a complex list, which is possible but unlikely.

L11.why: Progressive 'were hauling' is the odd form out; any of the four could match some subject and time frame.

L12.why: Number and voice depend on the hidden subject; all four can be correct somewhere.

L13.why: Active past perfect 'had actually brought' needs an object and earlier-past frame; none is impossible.

L14.why: No punctuation may fuse two elements, but 'magnification deep in the tissue' shows it can be correct.

L15.why: Past perfect is the least likely, but base, past, past perfect and participle forms each fit some construction.

L16.why: Perfect participle 'having left' is the least common fit; every form fits some sentence structure.
